*Tōh. 366*. *Ka* 151b1–193a. *Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījālasaṃvara* (The Union of All Buddhas: The Vajra Net of Ḍākinīs).
Dalton-van Schaik 2006, 454/1 (in quotations) & 716/2 (deities);
van Schaik’s *Early Days* contains some discussion of this,
as does Weinberger 2003, though both appear rather confused.
% Davidson 1981 (reference not located by van Schaik) % Sanderson 2009: 145–156

For an early attestation, see the *Prajñāpāramitānayādhyardhaśatikāṭīkā* (*'Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa tshul brgya lnga bcu pa'i 'grel pa*; Toh. no. 2647), Dergé Tanjur, vol. JU, folios 272v.7–294r.5. — Davidson, IEB, pp. 242–243. — Yukio Hatta, *Index to the Ārya-Prajñāpāramitā-Naya-Śatapañcaśaṭīkā*, Heirakuji-shoten (Kyoto, 1971). — Shuyu Kanaoka, “Kukurāja,” *Indogaku Bukkyōgaku Kenkyū*, vol. 15, no. 1 (December 1966), pp. 8–17.

A translation of this commentary by Jñānamitra is already mentioned in the *Ldan/lhan kar ma* catalogue (cf. Lalou 1953: 331, no. 523: *tshul brgya lnga bcu’i ’grel pa | slob dpon Jñānamitras mdzad pa | 600 śl. | 2 bp ||*). This catalogue is commonly assigned to the reign of Khri lde srong btsan/Sad na legs, i.e., circa 800–815 CE (Halkias 2004: 48), though the dating is not uncontroversial (see ibid., n. 4). Jñānamitra’s work contains a narrative summarized by Weinberger (2003: 235–237) involving Indrabhūti and the siddha Kukkurāja. The *Sarvabuddhasamāyoga* is discussed here. [NB: The translation, even as preserved in more modern *gsar ma* canons, definitely has an archaic feel to it. This is evident not only from the way Sanskrit words are transcribed (very reminiscent of the haphazard Dunhuang fashion: e.g., *de byi* for *devī*, *guhya samanytsa* for *Guhyasamāja*, etc.), but also from archaisms such as the *-o cog* plural. Much of this is also discussed in IEB 242–245. Elements of the story (namely, Indrabhūti’s accomplishment with his harem) are alluded to in the *CMP* (ed. Wedemeyer, p. 477: *... yoginībhiḥ saha ramamāṇo yathā rājā Indrabhūtiḥ tadvat kalevaraṃ parivartya vajrakāyo bhūtvāntaḥpureṇa sahāntardhāyāṣṭaguṇaiśvaryānvito buddhakṣetrād buddhakṣetraṃ gacchati |*).

Amoghavajra provides the title of this text in his catalogue (Taishō 869), which dates from 746–774 CE. Sanderson (2009: 145, n. 336; see also Tomabechi 2007) dates his knowledge of the text to between 741 and 746, during which time he was in Sri Lanka and possibly India.

The scriptural materials related to the *Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījālaśamvara* consist of two titles found in the sDe dge canon in volume Ka of the Tantra section (Toh. nos. 366 and 367) [= Peking Rgyud Ka, Ōtani nos. 8 and 9]. The first is the tantra in question in ten chapters (referred to here as an *uttaratantra*, likely by error), while the second is the *Sarvakalpasamuccaya* (referred to here as an *uttarottaratantra*) in five chapters (numbered 18 through 22). The latter must also be an original Indic work, as there exists a commentary upon it by Ānandagarbha, and several testimonia (quoted [though not yet traced] and mentioned once each in the *Caryāmelāpakapradīpa* and the *Tattvasiddhi*). According to the testimony of *Pramuditavajra* (see below) and Bu ston Rin chen grub, there existed yet another tantra of this cycle in seven chapters. Bu ston even states that in his own time (the early 14th century) there were rumors of an earlier translation of this text, but that it could no longer be found (*...sngar 'gyur par grags te da lta ma rnyed do*). This, it appears, accounts for the peculiar numbering of the *Sarvakalpasamuccaya*, as the seven chapters fill the gap between the ten chapters of the root tantra and the first chapter of the continuation tantra, which is numbered eighteen.

The exegetical materials related to the *Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījālaśaṃvara* are organized in the sDe dge canon within volumes Ra and La of the *Rgyud ’grel* section (Tōh. nos. 1659–1682) [corresponding to Peking *Rgyud ’grel* volumes Ya and Ra].

Tōh. 1659 [= Ōta. 2531] is the longest commentary, attributed to one Brgya byin sdang/sdong po (*Indranāla)—according to the testimony of the colophon, a king from Oḍiyāna—but this is most likely not a translation of an Indic work, but rather a Tibetan composition. The author cites several tantras that are otherwise unknown in Indic sources but are very popular in the rNying ma tradition (such as the *Thabs kyi zhags pa*).

Tōh. 1660 [= Ōta. 2532] is a *vṛtti by *Pramuditavajra. At present, little is known of this author; however, he is likely not from a very early period, as he already knows of and discusses the notorious fourth initiation (*caturthābhiṣeka*). He also refers to earlier commentators, namely Ānandagarbha and *Praśāntamitra.

Tōh. 1661 [= Ōta. 2533] is attributed in its colophon to one of the Indrabhūtis as the author of the *Pañjikā; however, judging from the opening verses, it appears highly probable that the composition is actually the work of Śākyamitra, based on his inquiries to the aforementioned Indrabhūti.

Tōh. 1662 [= Ōta. 2534] is a commentary on the *Sarvakalpasamuccaya*, the *Uttaratantra*, by the renowned exponent of Yogatantra, Ānandagarbha (active in the 9th century). If the colophon statement is authentic, the work was composed at Nālandā. There is some circumstantial evidence suggesting that Ānandagarbha also produced a commentary on the present text, though it is not available to us in any form.

*Tōh.* 1663 [= *Ōta.* 2535] is another *pañjikā*, composed by *Praśāntamitra*. He should likely not be confused with the translator who shares the same name. Indian traditions identify him as a disciple of Jñānapāda and a contemporary of Dīpaṃkarabhadra; thus, his period of activity most likely falls around the middle of the ninth century. He is also a commentator on the *Māyājāla* (*Tōh.* 2514) and the *Vajramaṇḍālaṃkāra* (*Tōh.* 2515). The dedicatory verses of these works are very similar to those in the commentary relevant here (all three likely contained the phrase *saha praśāntamitreṇa*). For the time being, I have found no cited or referenced text in his works that would place him later than the aforementioned period.
The three latter commentaries (Toh. nos. 1661–63) were all translated by individuals whose dates can be relatively safely assigned to the first half of the eleventh century.

Tōh. 1664–1671 [= Ōta. 2536–2543] are all attributed to the siddha Kukurāja; these are *sādhanas* and an initiation manual (*abhiṣeka-vidhi*). It is noteworthy that the latter also mentions the fourth initiation (*caturthābhiṣeka*). Tōh. 1672 [= Ōta. 2544] is a *gaṇacakra-vidhi* attributed to (an) Indrabhūti. This work has been partially translated and studied to some extent by Davidson (2002: 318–319). The remaining texts are all *sādhanas*, most of which are attributed to one *Hūṃkāravajra* (and variants of this name). An exception is another initiation manual, Tōh. no. 1679 [= Ōta. 2551], which is attributed to one *Ratnavajra*, possibly the same as the eleventh-century Kashmiri author. I would not favor this identification, because this *Ratnavajra* discusses and endorses the fourth initiation, whereas we know from the Kashmiri *Ratnavajra*'s other works and testimonia that he was not prepared to accept its existence and vigorously debated the "Eastern paṇḍitas" (whom he primarily meant to be Vāgīśvarakīrti), who were, at least to him, its chief proponents. It is notable that this *Ratnavajra* states in the second introductory verse that (by his time) the tantra and its system had almost disappeared (*kun tu nub po nyid mthong nas*), which is one of the reasons for his composing the manual.
Peking: vol. Ka, djvu page 182; contained in the rNying ma rgyud 'bum.

The Indian scholar Vajrahāsa and the translator of *sgyu ’phrul* (māyā), Sna Rin chen mchog, established [this text] through a final revision in accordance with the texts of the four commentaries. Regarding the *Buddhasamayoga*, it is said that there exists a tantra consisting of twenty-two chapters (*kalpa*) which is a single compilation; this is the *Daśabhūmi-tantra*. There exists a subsequent tantra (*uttara-tantra*) consisting of seven chapters, and a further subsequent tantra (*uttarottara-tantra*) consisting of a compendium of chapters. Furthermore, the *Vajrāsana-catuṣpīṭha-tantra* is a concordant tantra (*tantra-pratirūpaka*).

In the language of India: *Śrī-sarvabuddhasamayoga-ḍākinījālasaṃvara-nāma-uttaratantra*. In the language of Tibet: *Dpal sangs rgyas thams cad dang mnyam par sbyor ba mkha' 'gro ma sgyu ma bde ba'i mchog ces bya ba'i rgyud phyi ma* (The Subsequent Tantra called the Glorious Union of All Buddhas with the Ḍākinīs of the Illusory Net, the Supreme Bliss). Homage to the glorious Vajrasattva!

He who always abides in the supreme, delightful secret, which is the self of all.
Always present within all things.

*Pramuditavajra: the conduct of Hevajra, Padmanarteśvara, and Vairocana.
Having stolen away the supreme accomplishment of the Vajrins, the supreme glory from Lokeśvara,
and the supreme bliss from the Buddhas, he enjoys them.
From the Buddhas— from the Buddha!—
the supreme siddha of the Vajra-holder and the first glory of the world.
Having seized the supreme bliss of the joy of the Buddha, they enjoy it. 4.7
\versvege % *Pramuditavajra: Vajrasūryacaryā \vers
Having forcibly seized by means of his prowess the entire great sovereignty of all Buddhas throughout the three realms without exception, he enjoys it.
He enjoys the entire great sovereignty of the Buddhas throughout the three realms without exception.
Having seized [them] openly by the power of their skill, they make use of them. 4.8 ||
\versvege % *Pramuditavajra: The Conduct of the Supreme Steed \vers
Having drawn forth the great siddhi of all the Buddhas and supreme, ultimate sovereignty, he enjoys it; what need is there to mention other manifestations of power?
Having drawn together— that is, having drawn in— having taken away:
the great siddhi of all Buddhas,
the supreme and holy lords.
If one enjoys wealth after having plundered it from others, what need is there to mention other forms of property? (4.9)
*Pramuditavajra*: Having explained the goddess of the wisdom of supreme siddhi, [the text] now explains the goddess of the meditative concentration of worldly siddhi.
Harasiddhi is renowned for her association with human sacrifice (Pāṭan Nepāl, Ujjayinī, etc.).
Siddhalakṣmī is identical to Pratyaṅgirā (*Praśāntamitra*);
she forcibly seizes [wealth] by her power and bestows it upon her devotees.
From great power comes stable auspiciousness;
from seizing comes accomplishment, and from mindfulness comes joy;
even after having seized through the force of intimidation.
He bestows it with faith. 4.10 ||
*Pramuditavajra*: Having taught the accomplishment of the precious consort, [he now teaches] the accomplishment of sovereignty.
Having forcibly seized the entire sovereignty of the three worlds along with all the lords of the worlds,
he bestows it upon his devotees.
Having completely usurped the sovereignty of the three worlds without exception,
along with all the lords of the world,
by means of the power of his boldness,
He bestows it upon those who have faith. 4.11 ||
\versvege *Pramuditavajra: Having taught the accomplishment of sovereignty, [he teaches] the accomplishment of the Lord.
The supreme and highest sovereignty over Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.
It bestows [its fruit] quickly by drawing [the soul] toward itself; how much more so, then, other manifestations of power?
Is it "āśu" or "asau"? [The text reads:
"Or else another [term]"—the Great Indra who enters the void of Brahmā.
O supreme and holy lords,
if you were to seize [wealth] from all quarters and give it away swiftly,
what need is there to mention other enjoyments? (4.12)
*Pramuditavajra: Having taught the mundane accomplishments, [he now teaches] the supramundane accomplishments.
There is nothing he cannot give, nor is there anything he cannot do;
he bestows and accomplishes all the purposes and activities of the Buddhas.
And he bestows [it] for the sake of the Buddhas.
There is nothing that he does not give; there is no purpose of the Buddha that he does not accomplish.
It is both giving and the act of doing. 4.13
And having taken away the state of Buddhahood and the state of a bodhisattva, he bestows them [upon others].
How much more so, then, the other supernatural attainments and the various streams of supreme ritual actions?
If one were to seize even other Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and give them away as gifts, [the merit would be immeasurable].
What need is there to mention the supreme activities, the perfections, or other accomplishments? 4.14 ||
The successful Amoghaprasara, the destroyer of all armies.
Amoghaprasara,
the shatterer [of obstacles].
The universal monarch, the great accomplished master of all Buddhas, attains success.
The supreme siddhi is beyond doubt;
it utterly destroys all factions and is the great accomplishment of all Buddhas.
The universal monarch is fully accomplished. 4.15 ||
Through the *Sarvabuddhasamāyoga*, the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*, and the rest.
He is the one who sets in motion the great miraculous transformations of the supernatural powers of all the Buddhas.
Manifesting great supernatural power and transformations.
\vparal{\vcd] By the *Ḍākinī-māyā-saṃvara*, the union of all Buddhas, \samputa\ 9.1.6ef}
The great miraculous power of all Buddhas enters into its full manifestation. 4.16
In some places there is the great mind of awakening, and in others the conduct that follows accordingly.
In some cases, however, there is the supreme descent from among the Tuṣita gods.
The pause-sandhi between pādas.
\vvar{\vd avakramaṇam] \eme, apakramaṇam \cod} \vparal{\vo] A \samputa\ 9.1.7}

A portion of an exegetical commentary preserved in the *Sampuṭatilaka*: "‘In some places’ (*kvacid*) means ‘unspecified. Because of the penetration of one’s own mind, it is the ‘mind of awakening’ (*bodhicitta*). Because of the attainment of awakening for the sake of all beings, one is a ‘Bodhisattva. His conduct is ‘Bodhisattva-conduct’ (*bodhicaryā*). Since he follows [beings] without failing to reach them according to their nature, he is ‘an attendant’ (*anuga*). He exists in the form of the triad of brothers: Jayakara, Madhukara, and Sarvārthasādhaka. Through his form, there is the welfare of beings; his various manifestations are his ‘births. Since he arises from the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, as well as from the essence of beings, he is therefore pure and Samantabhadra. Thus, the noble Bodhisattva-conduct is ‘according to the attendant. “As before” (*pūrvavat*) means as previously described.

From the Tuṣita gods, all around, [comes] the supreme wheel; the supreme wheel of the deities of the mantra, the cause, which possesses various miraculous powers (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*). Furthermore, O sons of good family, it is "by the assembly of all Buddhas. An assembly (*samāja*) is a gathering (*melaka*). "Sukhāvatī, the supreme mind, Tuṣita"—O sons of good family, [this place] is like the world-system Sukhāvatī. Just as the world-system Sukhāvatī is adorned by the assembly of all Tathāgatas, so too the Blessed One, Śrī Padmanarteśvara, is surrounded on all sides by immeasurable Tathāgatas such as Śrī Vairocana; therefore, he is like the world-system Sukhāvatī. For that reason, there shall be the arising of the savior Padmanarteśvarī.
In some places, as great bodhisattvas,
they proceed in accordance with their conduct; in some places,
from among the Tuṣita gods...
The sublime one is utterly beyond transition. 4.17
In some cases, indeed, the birth was pure; in others, the departure from the city.
In some places there is the great journey toward enlightenment, and in some places the defeat of Māra.
*bodhi-yātrā* (the pilgrimage for awakening) [emended from *bodhe-yā((t))+*]. [Commentary]: *yā((t)+* is found in \cod7\recto. Parallel: \A\ \samputa\ 9.1.8.

A portion of the commentary preserved in the *Sampuṭatilaka* states: "The emergence is manifest as the producer of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*) and the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*). The mass of merit (*puṇyaskandha*) is his; its pollen is the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and their buds are the eighty minor marks. What is that [mass]? It is the manifest teacher and such qualities. Their collection is the chapter. The journeys to great enlightenment: because he does not harm the Bodhi through the form of Māra, or because he slays the minds of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, he is Māra; or Māra is Vajrarāga. Because he has destroyed the four Māras, he is the Conqueror of Māra."
In some places birth is completely pure;
in some places definitive emergence is manifest; and in some places he proceeds to great awakening.
Thus, he is completely victorious over Māra. 4.18 ||
In some places there is the perfect awakening to enlightenment; in some places, the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
And in some places, there was the refutation of the non-Buddhist outsiders in accordance with the Dharma.
[This is] by means of the Dharma of the non-Buddhists; and as it is said in the *Śrīsaṃvara*: (Q/R). Ms. A 104 verso.

*Sampuṭa* 9.1.9: In certain instances, Śākyamuni, having attained manifest enlightenment, [taught] the purity of liberation through the rejection of the grasping at phenomena and persons. For the sake of worldly yogins, he rejected the person (*pudgala*); for the sake of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, he rejected the grasping at phenomena (*dharma*). [Tibetan:
*byang chub mngon par rdzogs par sangs rgyas*].
In some places he turns the wheel of Dharma; in other places he subdues the non-Buddhist opponents in accordance with the Dharma. 4.19
In some places, there is the sovereignty over all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhīśvaratva*) and the glorious *Trilokavijaya*.

In some places, there is the sovereignty of the Lord of Accomplishments (*siddhīśvaratva*); and in others, the unsurpassed sovereignty of the accomplishment that is the foremost of all ritual manuals (*sarvakalpāgrya*).
[The attainment of] the sovereignty of supernatural powers,
unsurpassed.

Possibly some exegetical commentary survives in the *Sampuṭatilaka*: "The Lord of All Siddhis is Paramāśva. By that Vajrahūṃkāra, through the taking of the three refuges and so forth, Mahādeva and the others of the three worlds were uplifted and disciplined; his maṇḍala is the lifting up of the entire triple world. After Umā had been given as a teacher’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*) and Mahādeva had departed..."

And perhaps it continues elsewhere in the same text: "He obtains the name Vajra-hūṃkāra, the Uplifter of the Three Worlds; he becomes Vajrasattva, the Conqueror of the Three Worlds. Then, regarding "another": from among Lālita, Karuṇābala, and so forth, one of the wrathful deities (*krodha*) is chosen. Then, by means of that wrath, what is the name of this single, smokeless Wrathful One (*ekaniṃdhūrakrodha*), O Blessed One? For what purpose did he speak? They say it is for the sake of those who hold the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), grasping at a soul (*jīva*), a person (*pudgala*), and so on. This is the ender of all conceptual constructions (*kalpyanta*); having conquered the wheel of the enemy of conceptualization (*kalpāricakra*) of those [who hold such views], he himself shall become the supreme siddhi of all conceptualizations.
In some places he is the Victor over the three worlds,
the very lord of all accomplishments;
in some places he is the supreme of all conceptualizations.
The unsurpassed lord of siddhas. 4.20 ||
By means of these and other such commitments (*samvara*) of the essence of all Buddhas, which are infinite in extent, [one attains the goal].

"By means of these and other [pledges], beginning with these and ending with the infinite," said the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittavajra, regarding all the supreme vows of the Buddhas.
He dances with the playful transformations of the methods of discipline.
He dances,
and so forth,
with infinite excellence.
Through the emanations of Cakrasaṃvara, the self of all Buddhas, he joyfully sports in the definitive dance that serves as the means for taming beings. 4.21
The supreme great siddhi of all, the steadfast lord of great sovereignty.
The sovereign of form, longevity, strength, complexion, and glory, he was like another Vajrasattva.
The supreme among all great siddhis, [endowed with] longevity and strength.
Stable one, the master of great power, possessing form, longevity, complexion, and strength— glorious like Vajrasattva himself. 4.22
Being served by the worlds and likewise worshipped by the Tathāgatas, \versvege \vers sevyamāno jagadbhis tu pūjyamānas tathāgataiḥ\ledsidenote{\Td 155b} \dandab % |
The glorious Vajrasattva, the lord of all goddesses, is accomplished.
The glorious one is accomplished and should be venerated by all beings.
Worshipped by all the Tathāgatas,
the supreme glory of all goddesses,
one is perfectly accomplished as Vajrasattva. 4.23
Sealing the entire realm of sentient beings in its manifold ways, he— \versvege \vers\noindent\dandab %
Sealing it completely in manifold ways, he shall bestow upon sentient beings the firm, difficult-to-attain awakening that is free from death.
To bestow upon the many realms of sentient beings enlightenment that is difficult to achieve.
He seals everything without exception;
he firmly ripens gods and those who practice the difficult path of awakening within all sentient beings. 4.24
One would personally become all the kalpas, both those with remainder and those without remainder.
AG would read *-kalpān* as the nominative plural;
[is this] the accusative of duration meaning "for all kalpas"?
He accomplishes the welfare of all sentient beings through the vows that are the very essence of all Buddhas.
By means of the supreme bliss that is the self of all Buddhas,
one acts for the benefit of all sentient beings.
Without remainder and without leaving anything behind, he remains throughout all eons for the sake of existence. 4.25
\versvege \bigskip \startcomm
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the glorious Vajrasattva.
"O Bhagavān!
Thus spoke the Blessed One, Vajrasattva.
\commvege \bigskip \startcomm
From the *Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījālaśamvara*, the fourth chapter, the glorious *Samayakalpa* named "The Accomplishment of the Supreme Auspiciousness of All Universes."

This is the supreme accomplishment of the universal auspiciousness of all things, known as the "Supreme Accomplishment of the Good Fortune of All Varieties," from the *Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinīmāyāśrīparamasukha*. It is the fourth chapter, the Glorious Samaya-kalpa.
Chapter Five
For he is the Blessed One, the yoga of Vajrasattva, the Tathāgata.
For this indeed is the *Sarvabuddhasamāyoga-Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*.
This is the yoga of the Blessed One,
the Tathāgata Vajrasattva,
the union of all Buddhas.
The Ḍākinī Illusion, Supreme Bliss. 5.1
For he alone is truly perfected, being directed according to his will.
In all ritual procedures for the kalpas, this is the supreme, unsurpassed accomplishment.
The unique, unsurpassed accomplishment is applied according to one's desire.
In all ritual procedures involving conceptualization, this is the supreme among the most excellent accomplishments. 5.2
For those who desire various procedures through the application of diverse karmas, [this is taught].
For the sake of disciplining sentient beings and for the accomplishment of all happiness, [this is the method].
Through the application of various activities for the sake of discipline,
[one attains] the desire for various rituals.
For the sake of disciplining sentient beings and for the accomplishment of all happiness. 5.3.
That very Blessed One is Yoga, through the miraculous transformations of all the Buddhas.
"Blessed One! [he said.]
Manifesting for the sake of all sentient beings, one succeeds most swiftly.
O Vikurvan!
This very yoga of the Blessed One,
through the miraculous manifestations of all the Buddhas—
When there is a miraculous manifestation for the benefit of all sentient beings, it will be swiftly and perfectly accomplished. 5.4
Either daily, or monthly, or likewise annually.
Or alternatively, one should perform the dance of the Buddha-saṃvara according to the prescribed ritual foundation.
He receives empowerment from the Buddhas.
\vparal{\vo] Q/R \cmp\ (xx) • \vajradaka 36.1cde} % Q/R (śrīsaṃvare) in Caryāmelāpakapradīpa % some exegesis surviving in \vajradaka\ 50. (\T 106\recto-\verso)
Whether it be every day, or every month,
or likewise every year,
having blessed [it] accordingly,
One should perform the dance of Buddha Saṃvara. 5.5
Or likewise, with [images] made of all kinds of minerals, or similarly made of jīvamūla.
\vparal{\vab] \vajradaka 36.3ab} % jīvamūla: bone?
% BraYā: animal, vegetable, mineral, see chapter 7
Accomplished through the faces of one's own deities, it is the dancing of the mudrās.

[The goddess] was made to dance; [this is] the manifestation of the *cihnamudrā* (symbol-seal) [pertaining to] one's own presiding deity. *(Note: An emendation is suggested; the manuscript reads *siddhimudrāpravartanam*, while the Tibetan translation, according to W., suggests *siddhamudrāpravartanam*.)*
Incorporated in Bhūvācārya’s *Saṃvarodaya* 349, cf. verse 528ab with glosses:
"the nature of all the elements" (as placeholders).
Likewise, arising from the vital breath and the channels,
one should thoroughly perform the mudrā of the sādhana in the form and attire of one's own deity. 5.6
Whichever maṇḍala one should enter by means of the offering to Viśvamudrā, [that very one shall be attained].
Having performed each of those [rites] while being honored by all the groups of disciples, he should cause it to be paid with great honor.
Should one celebrate? One should perform a festival (*utsavaṃ kuryāt*). Or [use] the causative of the root *mah-*:
*pūjayan*! If one wishes to be precise, however, one should note that *pūjayan* occurs in other instances as well (three such occurrences have been identified thus far).
In whatever mandala is relied upon,
with the offering of various mudrās,
all the assemblies of disciples [should be placed] right there.
Having performed worship, one should accomplish it through that. 5.7

A portion of the commentary preserved in the *Sampuṭatilaka* states: "Through the gift in which the giver, the recipient, and the act of giving are not perceived, there is the abandonment of stinginess; this is ultimate purity (*paramārthaviśuddhi*). For that purpose—and in order to engage all beings in perpetual giving through the knowledge of the complete purity of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍalapariśuddhi*)—the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) resembling the sun is the 'Sun Great Seal' (*sūryamahāmudrā*). Regarding "Ākāśagarbha": space (*ākāśa*) is the gnosis of equality (*samatājñāna*), and he whose "womb" (*garbha*)—that is, his cause of origination—is that, is so called. Because he is the lord of all supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), he is the "Fulfiller of All Hopes. The hopes of all sentient beings consist of their prayers for every kind of sovereignty, such as that of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*); because he grants these, he is the "Fulfiller of All Hopes. Therefore it is said: "From space, the excellent jewels such as women, the producer of all jewels"—meaning the producer of the seven jewels. For this reason, Tārā becomes the "Conqueror of the Three Worlds" (*trailokyavijaya*).

Regarding the surviving exegesis in the *Sampuṭatilaka*: "What is this 'seated on a skull' (*kapālāsana*) upon which the goal is to be accomplished? For that is established by its very nature, through its power (*prabhāva*) and intrinsic being (*svabhāva*). Power is efficacy, the state of being free from the conceptualization of subject and object. By that very reality of power, it is established by nature. Its form as a crown of garlands of skulls is its intrinsic being (*svabhāvaka*), because of non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*). This is what is meant: just as the heat of fire is established by its very nature, so too, for him, there is natural purity (*prakṛtiviśuddhi*) through power alone. Having performed the yoga of the pledge of true reality (*sutattvāsamayayoga*), there is union with all gnosis. Such a yoga is to be understood as belonging to all the Tathāgatas and others.

Some exegetical commentary preserved in the *Sampuṭatilaka*: In meditation, one should fix the gaze upon the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) and visualize Gaurī as being raised up. Having entered the heart of the object of accomplishment with the mind, one should draw out his heart-lotus with the left hand by means of attraction. Caurī, through the mental visualization of kissing the face of the object of accomplishment, brings about delusion; she deludes him directly by means of the "deluding-face" (*pramoha-mukha*). Vettālī embraces the dead and causes them to rise; having mentally unified herself with the object of accomplishment, she then makes him dance. By means of the yoga of Pukkasī, she makes him dance; having become one with the object of accomplishment through the mind, she should cause the upward gaze to occur by means of "face-delusion. By means of the yoga of Caṇḍālī, she kills. With all possible applications and various types of activities,

\commvege \bigskip \vers The wise man, having understood the nature of the world, does not grieve;

for he knows that all conditioned things are subject to change and destruction. Just as a rain-cloud, having gathered, eventually disperses, so too do all formations dissolve. Having seen this with wisdom, the sage remains free from sorrow. He understands that birth, old age, sickness, and death are the inherent nature of all beings. Therefore, having abandoned attachment to the self and what belongs to the self, he dwells in peace, having transcended all worldly concerns. Just as a lamp flickers and goes out when its oil is exhausted, so too does the mind of the one who has realized the truth find liberation through the cessation of craving. filling, projecting, and clarifying. With the feet pressed together, one treads upon the earth.
One should seal the earth with the *bhū-mudrā* by placing the feet evenly; one should seal the intermediate space (*bhuvas*) with the *vaiśākha-mudrā*.

[May there be] well-being;
[the posture] ālīḍha.
With legs extended, he treads upon the earth; the mandalas as well shall be trampled. By extending and contracting [the limbs], he treads upon the three places.

Lack of laxity, steadfastness, softness, and firmness of limb.

[The bow] drawn to its full extent,

Fever, poisons, artificial toxins, diseases, the afflictions of *ḍākinīs*, and planetary influences.

The Seal of the Full Abode.
This is the mudrā of extensive filling.

Drawing the bow with ease as if leading it to one's own heart,

then, having formed fists, the index fingers should be well drawn inward.

Now, this knowledge of the mudrās, which is entirely universal,
I shall proclaim through the yoga that is entirely universal.
Then, having also accomplished the knowledge of this Viśvāmudrā,

Just as by the dancing of possession and by the release of all mudrās, \vers * \dandab * \ledsidenote{\Td 192b} \veg
By dancing with the eyebrows, eyes, teeth, and lips, and with the mouth, body, and hands,
according to the prescribed manner, one completely releases all mudrās. 10.2
The union with Śrīvajrasattva, through the assemblies of all goddesses,
becomes successful as the one who is auspiciously beautiful in every respect.
Through the union with glorious Vajrasattva, the assembly of all goddesses will bring about the attainment of supreme bliss,
which is everywhere manifold and auspicious. 10.3
By this very seal of empowerment, one is blessed by all the Buddhas;
through self-empowerment, the assembly of all the Buddhas truly comes to be.
If one seals with this mudrā, all the Buddhas will bestow their blessing;
once they have been properly blessed, all the Buddhas will appear. 10.4
Through the union with all Buddhas, one becomes composed of all Buddhas;
and because of being composed of all Buddhas, one accomplishes the state of all Buddhas.
Through union with all Buddhas, one becomes equal to all Buddhas;
because one is equal to all Buddhas, all Buddhas are perfectly accomplished. 10.5
By the power of the union with Śrī Vajrasattva alone,
all mudrās are themselves realized in every respect; this is the summary.
By the very power of the glorious union with Vajrasattva,
in short, all mudrās are accomplished individually in every respect. 10.6
And they reveal their entire selves, with forms that are truly enchanting; they grant shouts of "Well done! along with perfected boons.

All self-perfections are delightful and fulfill all hopes; through enjoyment according to one's desire, [all selves...]

bestows the very self of all things as whatever enjoyments one desires. 10.8.10.8
And he, whose self is all things, honors [the Buddha] with the outpourings of all his senses,
through the vast and accumulated arrays of great clouds of every kind of offering.

This is the complete accomplishment of all mudrās of Vajrasattva; it is swiftly accomplished.
Siddhis will surge upward, and vast activities will be swiftly accomplished. 10.11
Having sealed the three realms in their entirety with this mudrā,
that which is sealed, deluded, and consumed— even if reduced to ashes—
shall be restored to life.

The limits of the power and qualities of this [deity], which are infinite and boundless, and of all conceptualizations, cannot be fully expressed. 10.16
For he is indeed accomplished by his very nature, through his power and inherent character;
thus he acts in accordance with that.
Established by power and by nature, it is perpetually established by its very essence;
it bestows bliss through individual accomplishment—this is the supreme secret, the highest of the high. 10.17
For the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, and not for the sake of purifying their own karma,
the Victors perform acts of purification.
There is no obstacle here, nor indeed are there Māras; success is established for an eon, sustained by non-decline.
[Upajāti meter:
For the sake of sentient beings, the Victorious One does not cease from engaging in activities nor from [ensuring their] complete purification.
In this, there are no obstacles, nor even any Māras;
liberation cannot be achieved through conceptual thought, nor can it ever be attained by such means. 10.18
I do not fall into the state of Māra, nor do I succumb to lack of firmness;
for the sake of firmness, I do not teach with a desire for gain.
May I quickly become firm for the sake of supreme, excellent enlightenment— that [enlightenment] which one who would accomplish it seeks not through his own pleasures, but through sufferings.
I do not become a Māra for those who are steadfast,
nor do I instruct them for the sake of making them steadfast.
Whoever seeks me through their own happiness, I shall grant them my supreme accomplishment. 10.19
Thus spoke he who is manifold in every way.
The Blessed One, the Tathāgata, was eternally joyful;
he praised and became exceedingly delighted by the well-spoken words of the glorious Vajrasattva. 10.20

*... [With] various offerings of lotuses of passion and attachment, and by clearly honoring with the bliss of the supreme horse-yoga, ...*
Through the supreme yoga of great bliss,
the most excellent joy of the fortunate, one will achieve the accomplishment of the samaya, which is the nature of the most sublime bliss.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the glorious Vajrasattva.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, Śrī Vajrasattva.
[Colophon] Thus ends the *Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījālasamvara*, known as the *Supreme Bliss of the Ḍākinī Illusion*, the great wheel-turner of all ritual manuals (*kalpa*), the Great Bliss.
[End of commentary]
